scope.domain: low-wage labor markets with monopsony power or employer concentration

qualifier.context: based on recent natural experiments (e.g., Card & Krueger, Cengiz et al.) showing neutral or positive employment effects

C005.subject: raising the minimum wage by a moderate amount (e.g., 10-20%) in labor markets with monopsony power
C005.object: increased employment among teenagers and low-skilled workers due to reduced wage-setting power of employers
evidence_refs: [Simulated evidence for: raising the minimum wage by a moderate amount (e.g., 10-20%) in labor markets with monopsony power increased employment among teenagers and low-skilled workers due to reduced wage-setting power of employers]

[PATH:empirical] Quasi-experimental studies using border discontinuities (e.g., Dube, Lester, & Reich 2010) that compare employment outcomes for teenagers and low-skilled workers in contiguous counties with different minimum wage levels, stratified by local employer concentration (Herfindahl-Hirschman Index). — Such studies can directly test whether moderate minimum wage increases lead to employment gains specifically in high-monopsony markets, by exploiting exogenous variation in wage floors and measuring heterogeneous effects across labor market concentration levels.

[PATH:theoretical] Structural estimation of monopsony power using firm-level labor supply elasticities (e.g., Manning 2003; Webber 2015) applied to low-wage sectors, combined with simulated policy counterfactuals of a 10-20% minimum wage increase. — This approach can confirm the mechanism by estimating the degree of wage-setting power employers hold and predicting employment responses under the monopsony model, providing a rigorous test of the causal chain from reduced monopsony power to increased employment.

[PATH:literature] Meta-analysis of minimum wage studies that code for local labor market monopsony indicators (e.g., number of employers per worker, job-to-job transition rates) and test for effect moderation. — Synthesizing existing empirical evidence with a focus on market structure heterogeneity can reveal whether the predicted positive employment effect is consistently found in high-monopsony contexts, thereby confirming or refuting the hypothesis across multiple settings.

scope.domain: low-wage labor markets characterized by high employer concentration and limited worker mobility

qualifier.mechanism: monopsony model predicts that wages below competitive equilibrium can be raised without employment loss

C006.subject: raising the minimum wage by a moderate amount (e.g., 10-20%)
C006.object: no measurable increase in unemployment among teenagers and low-skilled workers, and potentially increases employment through efficiency wage effects and reduced turnover
evidence_refs: [Simulated evidence for: raising the minimum wage by a moderate amount (e.g., 10-20%) no measurable increase in unemployment among teenagers and low-skilled workers, and potentially increases employment through efficiency wage effects and reduced turnover]

[PATH:empirical] Re-analysis of Card and Krueger (1994) and subsequent replication studies using modern difference-in-differences methods with synthetic controls and border discontinuities — This directly tests the hypothesis in the specified scope (monopsonistic labor markets) by examining whether moderate minimum wage increases in contiguous state pairs with differing wage policies lead to no measurable unemployment effects, while also testing for efficiency wage effects via reduced turnover.

[PATH:empirical] Firm-level panel data studies on minimum wage impacts in low-wage industries (e.g., fast food, retail) that measure both employment and turnover rates before and after policy changes — Provides direct evidence on the efficiency wage channel: if turnover declines and employment remains stable or increases, it supports the hypothesis. If turnover is unchanged but employment falls, it refutes the hypothesis.

[PATH:literature] Meta-analysis of quasi-experimental minimum wage studies from 2010-2020, focusing on studies that explicitly model labor market concentration (monopsony power) as a moderating variable — Synthesizes existing evidence to assess whether the hypothesized null effect on unemployment holds specifically in monopsonistic settings, and whether efficiency wage effects are consistently observed across contexts.

scope.domain: monopsonistic labor markets where employers have wage-setting power

qualifier.context: based on modern quasi-experimental studies using difference-in-differences methodology across state borders (2010-2020)

C007.subject: raising the minimum wage by a moderate amount in markets with high employer concentration
C007.object: increased labor force participation among previously discouraged workers due to improved wage prospects
evidence_refs: [Simulated evidence for: raising the minimum wage by a moderate amount in markets with high employer concentration increased labor force participation among previously discouraged workers due to improved wage prospects]

[PATH:empirical] Quasi-experimental study comparing labor force participation rates in high-concentration local labor markets (e.g., retail/food service) before and after a moderate minimum wage increase, using synthetic control methods or difference-in-differences with matched non-increase regions. — Directly tests the causal claim by leveraging variation in minimum wage policy across similar monopsonistic markets, isolating the effect on discouraged workers' re-entry.

[PATH:empirical] Survey-based longitudinal analysis of discouraged workers' job search behavior and reservation wages in high-employer-concentration industries, pre- and post-minimum wage change, to assess whether wage improvements reduce non-participation. — Provides micro-level evidence on the proposed mechanism (reservation wage barrier reduction) and its link to labor force participation, complementing aggregate estimates.

scope.domain: low-wage labor markets with monopsony power, particularly in retail and food service sectors

qualifier.mechanism: higher wages reduce reservation wage barriers and make employment more attractive relative to non-participation

C008.subject: raising the minimum wage by a moderate amount
C008.object: significant disemployment effects concentrated among the least-skilled workers and youngest job seekers
evidence_refs: [Simulated evidence for: raising the minimum wage by a moderate amount significant disemployment effects concentrated among the least-skilled workers and youngest job seekers]

[PATH:empirical] Clemens, J. (2021). 'How Do Firms Respond to Minimum Wage Increases? Understanding the Relevance of Non-Employment Margins.' Journal of Economic Perspectives, 35(1): 51-72. — Provides direct evidence on firm-level adjustments (e.g., reduced hours, substitution of labor) that can reveal whether disemployment effects are concentrated among least-skilled and youngest workers, helping confirm or refute the hypothesis.

[PATH:empirical] Cengiz, D., Dube, A., Lindner, A., & Zipperer, B. (2019). 'The Effect of Minimum Wages on Low-Wage Jobs.' Quarterly Journal of Economics, 134(3): 1405-1454. — Uses a border discontinuity design to estimate employment effects of minimum wage changes, with subgroup analyses for teens and low-skilled workers, directly testing the claimed concentration of disemployment.

[PATH:literature] Neumark, D. & Shirley, P. (2022). 'Myth or Measurement: What Does the New Minimum Wage Research Say About Minimum Wages and Job Loss in the United States?' NBER Working Paper 30487. — A comprehensive meta-analysis that synthesizes recent evidence on minimum wage effects, specifically examining heterogeneity by skill level and age, providing a rigorous check on the hypothesis's scope and confidence.

scope.domain: competitive labor markets with elastic labor demand, particularly affecting teens, young adults without college education, and workers with minimal experience

qualifier.context: based on CBO estimates showing 1.3 million job losses from $15 minimum wage, Neumark & Wascher meta-analyses, and evidence that aggregate employment effects mask substitution toward more-skilled workers

C009.subject: raising the minimum wage to 150% of the local median wage
C009.object: complete offset of job losses through productivity gains in high-turnover retail and food service sectors within 18 months
evidence_refs: [Simulated evidence for: raising the minimum wage to 150% of the local median wage complete offset of job losses through productivity gains in high-turnover retail and food service sectors within 18 months]

[PATH:empirical] Natural experiments comparing employment and productivity metrics in U.S. cities that implemented large minimum wage increases (e.g., Seattle, $15/hour) vs. matched control cities, with panel data on turnover costs and output per worker in high-turnover retail and food service firms. — Directly tests the claim by observing actual employment changes and productivity offsets in the specified sectors under real wage shocks, controlling for local economic conditions.

[PATH:empirical] Firm-level longitudinal studies tracking hiring, training costs, worker tenure, and sales per employee in high-turnover establishments before and after minimum wage hikes, using administrative payroll and productivity data (e.g., from Bureau of Labor Statistics or state unemployment insurance records). — Allows estimation of whether reduced turnover costs and improved worker effort compensate for higher wages, and whether net employment effects are neutral or positive within 18 months.

[PATH:literature] Meta-analysis of existing literature on minimum wage effects in low-wage service sectors, focusing on studies that measure productivity channels (e.g., efficiency wage theory, training substitution) and turnover rates, to assess the plausibility and magnitude of full offset. — Synthesizes prior evidence to evaluate whether the hypothesized mechanism has empirical support across different contexts and timeframes, identifying conditions under which offset might occur or fail.

scope.domain: retail and food service establishments with baseline annual turnover rates exceeding 75%

qualifier.mechanism: reduced hiring and training costs combined with increased worker effort and experience retention create net positive employment effects

C010.subject: raising the minimum wage
C010.object: accelerated automation adoption and reduced hiring of entry-level workers, creating net employment losses that productivity gains cannot offset
evidence_refs: [Simulated evidence for: raising the minimum wage accelerated automation adoption and reduced hiring of entry-level workers, creating net employment losses that productivity gains cannot offset]

[PATH:empirical] Quasi-experimental studies comparing employment and automation adoption rates in fast-food and retail firms across U.S. states with differing minimum wage increases (e.g., border county designs or synthetic control methods) — Directly tests the causal link between minimum wage hikes and capital substitution by isolating variation in wage floors from other economic factors, providing high-quality evidence on net employment effects.

[PATH:empirical] Longitudinal firm-level panel data from low-wage service industries tracking investment in automation technologies (e.g., self-service kiosks, automated ordering systems) alongside hiring and hours data before and after minimum wage changes — Allows measurement of whether automation adoption accelerates specifically in response to wage floors and whether resulting productivity gains fail to compensate for reduced entry-level hiring, addressing the core substitution and offset claims.

[PATH:theoretical] Task-based theoretical models of labor demand with endogenous automation (e.g., Acemoglu & Restrepo framework) calibrated to low-wage service sector data — Provides a formal mechanism to test whether productivity gains from automation are insufficient to offset labor demand reductions under realistic wage floor scenarios, helping to reconcile conflicting empirical findings and identify boundary conditions.

scope.domain: low-wage service industries with automatable tasks

qualifier.context: firms respond to wage floors by substituting capital for labor and reducing workforce expansion, as observed in fast food and retail sectors post-minimum wage increases
